name: Clement of Alexandria
status: Church Father. Kept by some Anglican churches, not on the Catholic or Orthodox calendars.

seo.title: Clement of Alexandria: is he a saint? Life, quotes and feast day
seo.description: Clement of Alexandria in plain words: Origen's teacher, his best lines with book and chapter, and why Rome left him off its calendar.

band.lede: A teacher at Alexandria who wanted Christians to learn from the Greek philosophers, and called the whole of life a festival.

picture.alt: An engraved portrait of an old, bearded Clement seated in a high-backed chair, wrapped in a heavy cloak, turning to speak with one hand raised.
picture.credit: Clement of Alexandria, from André Thevet, Les vrais pourtraits et vies des hommes illustres, 1584. Boston Public Library. Public domain.
picture.creator: André Thevet

card.line: A teacher at Alexandria who wanted Christians to learn from the Greek philosophers, and called the whole of life a festival.

filters.alias: clemens alexandrinus titus flavius stromata stromateis

who: Clement was a Christian teacher in Alexandria, Egypt, around the year 200. He led the church's school there, and the young Origen was among his pupils. He wanted Christians to read Greek philosophy without fear. His books range from God becoming man to when to laugh. No one recorded how or where he died.

roles.name: Helper
roles.line: To a bishop in prison, about 211

numbers.src: Miscellanies, Book 1, chapter 1, as McGiffert and Westcott count them
Catholic Encyclopedia; McGiffert, notes to Eusebius

lines: Four survive, in full or nearly
The rest are lost, or in pieces

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 150, probably at **Athens**. Even in the 300s, some said Alexandria.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: Nothing is recorded of his parents. He had a wide Greek education, and knew the pagan poets and philosophers well. He became a Christian as an adult, by his own choice.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: Between about **211 and 215**. No one recorded where, or how.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Titus Flavius Clemens**, his full name. In Latin, **Clemens Alexandrinus**. Cassiodorus calls him the Stromateus, the man of the Miscellanies.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: Church Father. A presbyter (a priest) of Alexandria, never a bishop. Kept by Anglicans in North America. Not on the Catholic or Orthodox calendars. Coptic writers call him St Clement.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: No likeness from his lifetime survives, and he has no fixed sign. A 1584 engraving shows an old bearded scholar in a chair. Ingres drew him in 1842 with a halo, and labelled him a bishop.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: The **Exhortation to the Greeks**, the **Instructor** in three books, the **Miscellanies** (Stromata) in seven, and **Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?** Eusebius lists ten works. The rest are lost, or survive in pieces.

portrait.alt: Ingres's design for a church window: Clement stands haloed under a painted arch, arms raised in prayer, in white robes and a rose vestment, above a plaque reading S. CLEMENS ALEXANDRINVS EPISCOPVS.
portrait.credit: Saint Clement of Alexandria, Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres, 1842. A design for a window of the Chapelle Saint-Ferdinand, Paris. Musée du Louvre. Public domain.
portrait.creator: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
portrait.caption: Ingres's design for a church window in Paris, 1842. The plaque calls him a bishop, which he never was. Musée du Louvre. Public domain.

west.text: The **Anglican Church of Canada**, in its Book of Common Prayer (1962). It was also his day in the **old Western martyrologies**, such as Usuard's, until the Roman Martyrology left him out.
The **Episcopal Church**, the **Anglican Church in North America** and the **Anglican Church of Canada**, in its Book of Alternative Services. Not the **Church of England**.

feasts.note: No Catholic, Orthodox or Lutheran calendar keeps a day for him. The Coptic Synaxarium has two other Clements, but not him. Beware 23 and 24 November: those are the days of Clement of Rome.

traits.title: took truth where he found it
traits.text: He would not tie himself to one school of philosophy. He took whatever each had said well, and called that mix philosophy. He had little patience with Christians who feared Greek learning: “the multitude are frightened at the Hellenic philosophy, as children are at masks”.

cite.text: Miscellanies, Book 1, chapter 7; Book 6, chapter 10

traits.title: grave and cheerful
traits.text: His rule book for Christians goes as far as laughter. He does not want it rooted out, only kept in bounds. “For man is not to laugh on all occasions because he is a laughing animal, any more than the horse neighs on all occasions because he is a neighing animal.”

cite.text: The Instructor, Book 2, chapter 5

traits.title: gentle with the rich
traits.text: His sermon on the rich opens by calling those who flatter the rich “godless and treacherous”. Then it tells rich believers that they can be saved. What they must give up, he said, is the love of money, not the money: “So let no man destroy wealth, rather than the passions of the soul, which are incompatible with the better use of wealth.”

cite.text: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?, sections 1 and 14

traits.title: open-handed
traits.text: He told givers not to sort the worthy from the unworthy. “Do not you judge who is worthy or who is unworthy. For it is possible you may be mistaken in your opinion.” Better to help the undeserving too than to miss someone God loves.

cite.text: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?, section 33

said.lede: His life is known from his own books and a few pages of Eusebius and Jerome. The warmest words come from his old pupil Alexander.

quotes.q: I have sent this letter to you by Clement, the blessed presbyter, a man virtuous and approved, whom ye yourselves also know and will recognize. Being here, in the providence and oversight of the Master, he has strengthened and built up the Church of the Lord.
quotes.who: Alexander, a bishop in prison for the faith and later bishop of Jerusalem, to the church at Antioch, about 211

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 11

quotes.q: Clement, a presbyter of Alexandria, in my judgment the most learned of men, wrote eight books of Miscellanies and as many of Outline Sketches, a treatise against the Gentiles, and three volumes called the Pedagogue. Is there any want of learning in these, or are they not rather drawn from the very heart of philosophy?
quotes.who: St Jerome, about two centuries later

cite.text: Jerome, Letter 70, to Magnus

quotes.q: In more recent times Clement has grown in favour for his charming literary temper, his attractive candour, the brave spirit which made him a pioneer in theology, and his leaning to the claims of philosophy. He is modern in spirit.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1908), Clement of Alexandria

moments.title: Six teachers, then rest
moments.text: He went looking for teachers, and he names none of them. His first was an Ionian, in Greece. Others he heard in southern Italy, and others in the East: one from Assyria, and a Hebrew in Palestine. Then he tracked down the last, hidden in Egypt, and went no further. “When I came upon the last (he was the first in power), having tracked him out concealed in Egypt, I found rest.” He calls him “the true, the Sicilian bee”. Eusebius takes this to be Pantaenus.

cite.text: Miscellanies, Book 1, chapter 1; Eusebius, Church History, Book 5, chapter 11, with McGiffert's notes; Wace, Dictionary of Christian Biography

moments.title: Head of the school
moments.text: Alexandria was the great city of learning in the ancient world. Its church had a school, where new Christians and curious pagans could hear the faith explained. Clement first helped Pantaenus there, then took his place.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 6; Catholic Encyclopedia

moments.title: A boy called Origen
moments.text: One of his pupils was a boy named Origen. The Episcopal Church calls Origen “the most eminent theologian of early Greek Christianity”. Another pupil was probably Alexander, later bishop of Jerusalem.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapters 6 and 14; Jerome, Lives, chapter 38

moments.title: Three books, three stages
moments.text: Some scholars see his three great books as three stages. The Exhortation is an appeal to pagans. The Instructor is a guide to daily Christian life. The Miscellanies are a rambling notebook of deeper teaching. Their Greek name means something like patchwork quilts. He says he planted them like a wild, wooded hill, with “a mixture of fruit-bearing and fruitless trees”, to hide the fruit from thieves.

cite.text: Miscellanies, Book 7, chapter 18; Catholic Encyclopedia; Freese, notes to Photius

moments.title: Persecution empties the school
moments.text: In 202 the emperor Severus began a persecution. Origen's father was beheaded. Soon no one was left in Alexandria to teach the faith, “as all were driven away by the threat of persecution”, says Eusebius. Clement left the city then, it seems. As far as we know, he never came back.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapters 1 to 3, with McGiffert's notes

moments.title: With a bishop in prison
moments.text: His old pupil Alexander was now a bishop in Cappadocia, and in prison for the faith. Clement was with him, and looked after his church. When Antioch chose a new bishop, Alexander wrote a letter of joy, and Clement carried it there.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 11; Catholic Encyclopedia

words.note: Clement's own books survive. These lines are from William Wilson's translation in the Ante-Nicene Fathers, 1885.

feature.kicker: From his appeal to the Greeks
feature.q: The Word of God became man, that thou mayest learn from man how man may become God.
feature.ctx: It is an early form of what the Eastern churches call theosis: God became human so that humans might share in God's life. In Greek, {el|ὁ λόγος ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος γενόμενος, ἵνα δὴ καὶ σὺ παρὰ ἀνθρώπου μάθῃς, πῇ ποτε ἄρα ἄνθρωπος γένηται θεός.}

cite.text: Exhortation to the Greeks, chapter 1

quotes.q: Holding festival, then, in our whole life, persuaded that God is altogether on every side present, we cultivate our fields, praising; we sail the sea, hymning; in all the rest of our conversation we conduct ourselves according to rule.
quotes.who: His picture of the mature Christian. Conversation here means way of life.

cite.text: Miscellanies, Book 7, chapter 7

quotes.q: It is then, as appears, the greatest of all lessons to know one's self. For if one knows himself, he will know God; and knowing God, he will be made like God, not by wearing gold or long robes, but by well-doing, and by requiring as few things as possible.
quotes.who: Opening a chapter on true beauty.

cite.text: The Instructor, Book 3, chapter 1

quotes.q: Some men, in truth, live that they may eat, as the irrational creatures, “whose life is their belly, and nothing else.” But the Instructor enjoins us to eat that we may live.
quotes.who: The Instructor is his name for Christ.

cite.text: The Instructor, Book 2, chapter 1

quotes.q: The way of truth is therefore one. But into it, as into a perennial river, streams flow from all sides.
quotes.who: On why Christians may learn from Greek philosophy.

cite.text: Miscellanies, Book 1, chapter 5

quotes.q: He hath changed sunset into sunrise, and through the cross brought death to life; and having wrenched man from destruction, He hath raised him to the skies, transplanting mortality into immortality, and translating earth to heaven.

cite.text: Exhortation to the Greeks, chapter 11
The Instructor, Book 2, chapter 5

extras.title: Stories he passed on
extras.lede: Clement passed on stories about the apostles that had come down to him. Eusebius later copied both of these into his history.

items.title: John and the robber
items.text: He calls it “a tale, which is not a tale but a narrative”. The apostle John left a strong, handsome and eager young man in a bishop's care. The bishop baptised him, then relaxed his watch. The young man fell in with idle friends. In time he became the captain of a band of robbers, “the fiercest, the bloodiest, the cruelest”. John called for a horse and rode straight out. He did not run from the robbers' lookouts, and let them seize him. Their captain knew him, and ran in shame. The old apostle chased him, “forgetting his age”, and called out to him. The young man threw down his weapons and wept, and John brought him back to the Church.
items.quote: Why, my son, dost thou flee from me, thy father, unarmed, old? Son, pity me. Fear not; thou hast still hope of life. I will give account to Christ for thee.

cite.text: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?, section 42; Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 23

items.title: How the Gospels were written
items.text: Eusebius says Clement gave “the tradition of the earliest presbyters” on the Gospels. The Gospels with the family trees, Matthew and Luke, were written first. Mark wrote down what Peter had preached at Rome, because Peter's hearers asked him to. Peter neither stopped him nor urged him on. John wrote last of all.
items.quote: But, last of all, John, perceiving that the external facts had been made plain in the Gospel, being urged by his friends, and inspired by the Spirit, composed a spiritual Gospel.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 14, from Clement's lost Outlines

extras.title: What his critics say
extras.lede: Some of what Clement wrote has troubled readers ever since. Here are the main charges, each with his own words, and his defenders' answers where they give one.

items.title: Photius's list
items.text: In the 800s, Patriarch Photius of Constantinople read Clement's Outlines, a book now lost. He listed what he called “impious and legendary fables”. Among them: that matter has no beginning, that the Son is a creature, and that the Word only seemed to take flesh. He also found souls passing from body to body, and worlds before Adam. Yet he wondered if the worst was really Clement's. The Catholic Encyclopedia thinks Photius threw Clement's mistakes “into undue relief”.
items.quote: He talks much other blasphemous nonsense, either he or some one else under his name.

cite.text: Photius, Bibliotheca, codex 109; Catholic Encyclopedia

items.title: Did Christ need to eat?
items.text: Clement wrote that Jesus ate only so that those with Him would not get the wrong idea of Him, and that He felt neither pleasure nor pain. Photius accused him of Docetism, the belief that Christ only seemed human. The Catholic Encyclopedia says Clement “clearly admits in Christ a real body”, but thought it free of the common needs of life.
items.quote: For He ate, not for the sake of the body, which was kept together by a holy energy, but in order that it might not enter into the minds of those who were with Him to entertain a different opinion of Him.

cite.text: Miscellanies, Book 6, chapter 9; Catholic Encyclopedia

items.title: Free of all feeling
items.text: His perfect Christian is never angry or afraid, and does not even need cheerfulness. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls this “undoubtedly colored by Stoicism”. It is less a Christian with his feelings under control, it says, than “the ideal Stoic who has deadened his feelings altogether”.
items.quote: Nor does he need cheerfulness of mind; for he does not fall into pain, being persuaded that all things happen well.

cite.text: Miscellanies, Book 6, chapter 9; Catholic Encyclopedia

items.title: Run from persecution
items.text: He taught that Christians should not hand themselves over when persecution comes. Anyone who does, he says, shares the guilt of his own death. He left Alexandria himself when persecution came. Eusebius's editor, McGiffert, answers the charge of cowardice: “it was not unworthy cowardice which led Clement to take his departure”. Alexander's warm words show it, he says.
items.quote: If he who kills a man of God sins against God, he also who presents himself before the judgment-seat becomes guilty of his death.

cite.text: Miscellanies, Book 4, chapter 10; McGiffert, notes to Eusebius, Book 6, chapter 6

items.title: Rules for women
items.text: His Instructor has strict rules on dress for everyone, and stricter ones for women. Yet in the Miscellanies he says women and men, slave or free, are to practise every virtue alike, “since it is a fit consequence that the same nature possesses one and the same virtue”.
items.quote: Let her be entirely covered, unless she happen to be at home.

cite.text: The Instructor, Book 3, chapter 11; Miscellanies, Book 4, chapter 8

items.title: A hope for the dead
items.text: He held that Christ went down to Hades to preach the gospel, so that those who believed there could be saved. He saw God's punishments as meant to heal. Some modern writers count him among the first Christian universalists.
items.quote: …God's punishments are saving and disciplinary, leading to conversion…

cite.text: Miscellanies, Book 6, chapter 6; Wikipedia

myths.claim: His feast days are 23 November in the West and 24 November in the East.
myths.truth: Those are the days of another man, Clement of Rome. Britannica prints them under Clement of Alexandria. The Church of England and the Roman Martyrology keep Clement of Rome on 23 November, and Greek churches on 24 November. The one old Western day for Clement of Alexandria was 4 December.

cite.text: Britannica; Common Worship; the Roman Martyrology (1916)

myths.claim: Pope Sixtus V removed him from the Roman Martyrology in 1586.
myths.truth: Wikipedia says so, but gives no source. Pope Benedict XIV says Cardinal Baronius, who drew up the Roman Martyrology, simply did not carry his name over from the older lists. The Catholic Encyclopedia puts it under Pope Clement VIII.

cite.text: Benedict XIV, Postquam intelleximus (1748); Catholic Encyclopedia

myths.truth: He was a presbyter, or priest, and never a bishop. Ingres's window design calls him a bishop, but the ancient sources call him a presbyter.

cite.text: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 38; Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 11

myths.truth: No ancient source says so. Where and when he died is unknown. The last we hear of him alive, about 211, he is carrying a letter to Antioch.

cite.text: Wace, Dictionary of Christian Biography; Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 11

myths.claim: His letter about a Secret Gospel of Mark shows what he really taught.
myths.truth: The letter is known only from photographs of a copy that Morton Smith said he found at the Mar Saba monastery in 1958. The manuscript is now lost. Scholars still argue whether it is Clement's, a later forgery, or something else.

cite.text: Smith and Landau, The Secret Gospel of Mark (Yale, 2023); Wikipedia

myths.claim: He wrote the hymns “Sunset to sunrise changes now” and “Jesus our mighty Lord”.
myths.truth: Both are English hymns of the 1900s, built on his words: the first by Howard Chandler Robbins in 1939, the second by F. Bland Tucker. The Episcopal Church lists them among his writings.

cite.text: Hymnary.org; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022

stood.lede: Each line is Clement's own, from his books.

circle.name: Pantaenus
circle.text: His last teacher, and the one he stayed with. Clement first helped him at the school in Alexandria, then took his place.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 5, chapter 11, and Book 6, chapter 6

circle.name: Origen
circle.text: His pupil as a boy. Origen took charge of the teaching at Alexandria after Clement left. The Catholic Encyclopedia says Clement has been “dwarfed in history by the towering grandeur of the great Origen”.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapters 3 and 6; Catholic Encyclopedia

circle.name: Alexander of Jerusalem
circle.text: Probably his pupil, and a lasting friend. Clement helped his church while he was in prison. He dedicated a book to him, the Ecclesiastical Canon, or Against the Judaizers. Alexander wrote of him with deep affection after his death.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapters 11, 13 and 14

circle.name: Tatian and Carpocrates
circle.text: Rivals at two extremes. Tatian and Julius Cassianus taught that marriage was corrupt. The sect of Carpocrates and his son Epiphanes taught that wives should be shared. Clement answered both and defended marriage. The 1885 English edition left that whole book in Latin.

cite.text: Miscellanies, Book 3, chapters 2, 12 and 13

circle.name: Basilides and Valentinus
circle.text: Gnostic teachers who had taught at Alexandria. He answered their ideas on martyrdom and on death. He kept their favourite word, though: his name for a mature Christian is the Gnostic.

cite.text: Miscellanies, Book 4, chapters 12 and 13; Catholic Encyclopedia

circle.name: Jerome
circle.text: He admired Clement's learning two centuries later, and listed his books in his Lives of Illustrious Men.

cite.text: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 38; Letter 70

circle.name: Photius
circle.text: The patriarch of Constantinople in the 800s. He praised the Instructor and attacked the lost Outlines.

cite.text: Photius, Bibliotheca, codices 109 to 111

death.big: No one recorded how, when or where he died. He was alive about 211, and gone by about 215.
paras: The last we see of him, he is carrying Alexander's letter to Antioch, about 211.
A few years later, Alexander wrote to Origen about “those blessed fathers who have trodden the way before us”. Among them was “the holy Clement, my master and benefactor”.
No last words and no grave are recorded.

saint.big: It depends on the church. Anglicans in North America keep his day, and Coptic writers call him St Clement. He is not on the Catholic or Orthodox calendars.

churches.note: Left out of the Roman Martyrology
But no day in its Synaxarium
4 or 5 December, in the US and Canada
Not in the LCMS or ELCA calendars

paras: Doubts about his books are old. A list of books credited to Pope Gelasius put his works among those “in no case to be received amongst us”. In the 800s, Photius found errors in his lost Outlines.
The old Western martyrologies kept a St Clement on 4 December. When the Roman Martyrology was drawn up in the late 1500s, Cardinal Baronius did not carry the name over.

In 1748 Pope Benedict XIV looked at the case again, and did not add him. He gave three reasons. The old writers say almost nothing of his life. There is no trace that he was ever honoured in public. And some of his teaching was, at the least, open to doubt. Benedict said he meant no slight to Clement's learning.
Even so, the Catholic Encyclopedia of 1908 calls him St Clement, and Pope Benedict XVI gave a whole talk on him in 2007. The encyclopedia tells the older story like this:

quotes.q: Down to the seventeenth century he was venerated as a saint. His name was to be found in the martyrologies, and his feast fell on the fourth of December.
quotes.who: The Catholic Encyclopedia, 1908. It says he was dropped under Pope Clement VIII, on the advice of Baronius.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1908), Clement of Alexandria

prayer.intro: The Instructor closes with his own prayer to Christ, the Instructor, and then a hymn. These are the prayer's opening lines.
prayer.q: Be gracious, O Instructor, to us Thy children, Father, Charioteer of Israel, Son and Father, both in One, O Lord. Grant to us who obey Thy precepts, that we may perfect the likeness of the image, and with all our power know Him Who is the good God and not a harsh judge.

cite.text: The Instructor, Book 3, chapter 12
